title: AI Process Mining
shortDefinition: The extraction and analysis of event logs from enterprise systems to discover how business processes actually execute in practice — revealing process variants, bottlenecks, and deviations.
definition: AI process mining extracts and analyzes event logs from enterprise systems (ERP, CRM, BPM, ticketing systems) to discover exactly how business processes actually execute in practice — revealing the full range of actual process variants, bottlenecks, deviations, and inefficiencies that process maps drawn from interviews and assumptions never capture. The central insight of process mining is that what people think a process looks like and what it actually looks like in the data are often significantly different — and the data-driven picture is always more accurate.

sections.title: What process mining reveals
sections.description: Event logs capture the complete picture — all process variants, exceptions, and workarounds that documentation misses.

content.text: Traditional process documentation captures the intended process flow from workshops and interviews — the 'happy path' as stakeholders believe or want it to be. Event logs capture every case: the 60% that followed the expected path and the 40% that didn't, along with every exception, reroute, manual workaround, and unusual variant. AI process mining extracts this complete picture: how many process variants actually exist, where cases accumulate waiting, which steps produce the most rework, which process deviations correlate with worst outcomes, and where automation would eliminate the most manual touchpoints.

items: Complete picture — all variants, exceptions, and workarounds.
Variant count — how many actual paths exist.
Waiting time — where cases accumulate delay.
Rework hotspots — which steps produce most rework.
Deviation impact — which variants correlate with poor outcomes.
Automation opportunity — where manual touchpoints are highest.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: What people think a process looks like and what it actually looks like in the data are often significantly different — the data-driven picture is always more accurate.

sections.title: Key process mining applications
sections.description: Process discovery, conformance checking, performance analysis, process simulation, and continuous monitoring.

content.text: Process discovery — automated reconstruction of as-is process maps from event logs, providing a data-accurate baseline no documentation exercise achieves. Conformance checking — comparing actual process execution against intended process design, identifying where and how often the process deviates from policy. Performance analysis — quantifying where time and cost accumulate across the process, identifying the highest-impact bottlenecks for improvement investment. Process simulation — testing the impact of proposed process changes in simulation before implementation, using actual process data to model realistic outcomes. Continuous process monitoring — ongoing monitoring of process execution for deviations and emerging bottlenecks after improvement implementation.

items: Process discovery — data-accurate as-is process maps.
Conformance checking — identify policy deviations.
Performance analysis — quantify time and cost bottlenecks.
Process simulation — test changes before implementation.
Continuous monitoring — track execution and emerging issues.

content.title: Why it matters
content.text: Process mining should typically precede automation investment — it identifies which processes are worth automating and reveals the actual flow that automation needs to handle.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of AI process mining

content.text: AI process mining has limitations. Event log data quality is the primary constraint. Data availability varies across systems. Process variant complexity can be overwhelming without prioritization. Conformance checking only identifies deviations from documented processes. Performance analysis requires accurate case duration data. Continuous monitoring requires ongoing data extraction. Integration with automation tools adds complexity. Interpretation requires process domain expertise. Process mining reveals symptoms, not root causes.

items: Data quality — primary constraint for accuracy.
Data availability — varies across enterprise systems.
Variant complexity — can be overwhelming without focus.
Conformance limits — only identifies deviations from documented processes.
Case duration — requires accurate timestamp data.
Ongoing extraction — continuous monitoring requires it.
Integration complexity — with automation tools.
Domain expertise — required for interpretation.
Symptom vs. cause — reveals what, not why.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about AI process mining

items.question: How is process mining different from workflow automation?
items.answer: Process mining discovers and analyzes how processes actually work; workflow automation redesigns and automates them. Process mining should typically precede automation investment — it identifies which processes are worth automating and reveals the actual flow that automation needs to handle.

items.question: What ERP systems does process mining work with?
items.answer: SAP, Oracle, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and other systems that log timestamped events — the key requirement is accessible event log data with case IDs and timestamps.

items.question: How long does process mining analysis take?
items.answer: Initial discovery analysis: 6–12 weeks; ongoing monitoring infrastructure: 12–20 weeks.

items.question: Can process mining identify fraud or compliance violations?
items.answer: Yes — conformance checking identifies process deviations that may indicate fraud, segregation of duties violations, or policy non-compliance in audit-relevant processes.

items.question: What process types benefit most from process mining?
items.answer: High-volume transactional processes (order-to-cash, procure-to-pay, incident-to-resolution) with rich event log data and known variation in outcomes.

items.question: Can process mining help us make the case for automation investment?
items.answer: Yes — quantifying actual manual touchpoints, exception rates, and cycle time is precisely the business case data that automation investment decisions require.

items.question: What is conformance checking in process mining?
items.answer: Conformance checking compares actual process execution against intended process design — identifying where and how often the process deviates from policy or documented procedures.

items.question: Can process mining work with real-time data?
items.answer: Yes — continuous process monitoring infrastructure can extract and analyze event log data in near real-time, enabling proactive bottleneck and deviation detection.

items.question: Does process mining require data scientists?
items.answer: Process mining requires data engineering for extraction and preparation, but the analysis itself is increasingly supported by process mining platforms that surface insights visually — ClickMasters provides the technical capability alongside process domain expertise.
